doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Coltrane's ideals and Ornette's meticulous planning
summary: Discussion of Dixieland as collective improvisation, Coltrane's aims in Ascension, and the planning behind Ornette and the Art Ensemble.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Well Dixieland did the same thing.
Right, exactly. Yeah. Collaborative, spontaneous improvisation.
They were. They were taking chances.
Right. So I often times wonder if Coltrane thought that “Ascension” was a successful record. Maybe — I have not read whether or not his own opinion on it.
Well I think that Coltrane was going for some — I don’t think he ever made — I don’t know. It strikes me that he had an ideal in mind that no realization was ever going to

reach, he was never going to attain. I think Coltrane had some very high standards. And the marvelous thing about Coltrane is that he tried to — he went for them. And just by going for them, however short he falls of actually having us ascend, you know, he gives us a platform so that we can begin to see what “Ascension” might really be. He gives us some sort of lift and launch. It’s not all experimentation on those records either. I mean “Free Jazz,” they released a twenty minute version that Ornette did as a first take. And it has all of the structural guideposts that are actually in the record. Ornette knows very well what he does before he does it. I mean I’ve sat in on Ornette’s sessions. Ornette is a meticulous planner. And you can hear it even in the “Prime Time” stuff when it sounds like the sound is so large, there’s so many different things happening, but they end on a downbeat. How did that do that? Well Ornette knows exactly what’s happening. There is plenty of spontaneity but there’s no — and there’s surprises — but it’s not free of — it’s not just like a slice of okay now we’re going to blow and see what happens. The Art Ensemble also. Meticulously arranged and very smartly segued from episode to episode. And there was space to improvise within the episodes, but they had a lot of turning points, a lot of structural things in place. I don’t know who really does free jazz without any plan. I think that that’s an idea — that we can just get up and blow — is something that amateurs believe, and some of those amateurs have tried to turn their work into careers and I think they fall short. Because unless you have a sense of where you’re going, you’re not going to be able to deliver. It’s like taking a pizza out. Well I’m going to deliver it. I don’t know where I’m going to go. Well if you’re a pizza delivery guy — I do free delivery.
And no one’s going to enjoy it either.
